title: Benjamin Harrison
description: President of the United States from 1889 to 1893
wiki_lead:
Benjamin Harrison (August 20, 1833 – March 13, 1901) was the 23rd president of the United States, serving from 1889 to 1893. He was a member of the Harrison family of Virginia—a grandson of the ninth president, William Henry Harrison, and a great-grandson of Benjamin Harrison V, a Founding Father. A Union army veteran and a Republican, he defeated Democratic Party incumbent Grover Cleveland to win the presidency in the 1888 United States presidential election by winning the Electoral College while losing the popular vote. He was defeated by Cleveland in the 1892 United States presidential election, becoming the first president to be succeeded in office by his predecessor.
Harrison was born on a farm by the Ohio River and graduated from Miami University in Oxford, Ohio. After moving to Indianapolis, he established himself as a prominent local attorney, Presbyterian church leader, and politician. During the American Civil War, he served in the Union Army as a colonel, and was confirmed by the U.S. Senate as a brevet brigadier general of volunteers in 1865. Harrison unsuccessfully ran for governor of Indiana in 1876. In 1881, the Republican-controlled Indiana General Assembly elected Harrison to a six-year term in the Senate, where he served from 1881 to 1887.
Hallmarks of Harrison's administration were unprecedented economic legislation, including the McKinley Tariff, which imposed historic protective trade rates, and the Sherman Antitrust Act. Harrison also facilitated the creation of the national forest reserves through an amendment to the Land Revision Act of 1891. During his administration six western states were admitted to the Union. In addition, Harrison substantially strengthened and modernized the U.S. Navy and conducted an active foreign policy. His proposals to secure federal education funding as well as voting rights enforcement for African Americans were unsuccessful.
Due in large part to surplus revenues from the tariffs, federal spending reached $1 billion for the first time during his term. The spending issue in part led to the Republicans' defeat in the 1890 midterm elections. Cleveland defeated Harrison for reelection in 1892, due to the growing unpopularity of high tariffs and high federal spending. Harrison returned to private life and his law practice in Indianapolis. In 1899, he represented Venezuela in its British Guiana boundary dispute with the United Kingdom. Harrison traveled to the court in Paris as part of the case and after a brief stay returned to Indianapolis. He died at his home in Indianapolis in 1901 of complications from influenza.

grok_lead: Benjamin Harrison (August 20, 1833 â March 13, 1901) was an American lawyer, Civil War veteran, and Republican politician who served as the 23rd president of the United States from 1889 to 1893. Born in North Bend, Ohio, he was the grandson of William Henry Harrison, the ninth U.S. president who died after one month in office, making Benjamin the only grandson of a president to later hold the office himself. Harrison practiced law in Indianapolis, Indiana, after graduating from Miami University and studying under an apprenticeship, and rose to prominence as a colonel in the Union Army during the Civil War, commanding the 70th Indiana Infantry Regiment and earning a brevet promotion to brigadier general for gallantry at battles including Resaca and Nashville. Elected to the U.S. Senate from Indiana in 1881, Harrison lost renomination in 1887 but secured the Republican presidential nomination the following year, conducting one of the earliest "front-porch" campaigns from his Indianapolis home. He defeated incumbent Democrat Grover Cleveland in the 1888 election by capturing 233 electoral votes to Cleveland's 168, despite trailing in the popular vote by about 90,000 ballots out of over 11 million castâa rare instance of the electoral college overriding the popular will that underscored divisions over tariffs and civil service reform. Harrison's administration expanded federal authority through measures like the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890, the first federal law to prohibit monopolies and trusts, which he signed to curb corporate combinations restraining trade. It also enacted the McKinley Tariff, raising average import duties to nearly 50% to shield domestic industries amid post-war industrialization, though this contributed to higher consumer prices and Republican midterm losses in 1890. His tenure admitted six new statesâ North Dakota, South Dakota, Montana, Washington, Idaho, and Wyoming âmore than under any other presidency and shifting political power westward, while modernizing the Navy with new steel warships and establishing national forests under the Forest Reserve Act. Despite these legislative successes, Harrison's presidency faced criticism for extravagant federal spendingâearning the derisive label "Billion Dollar Congress" from opponentsâand failure to fully address economic discontent among farmers and laborers, factors that led to his defeat by Cleveland in the 1892 rematch. Post-presidency, Harrison argued landmark cases before the Supreme Court, including the income tax challenge in Pollock v. Farmers' Loan & Trust Co., and served briefly as counsel for Venezuela in its boundary dispute with Britain. His formal demeanor and focus on executive prerogative over party machines defined a transitional era bridging Gilded Age excess and Progressive Era reforms, though contemporary accounts often portrayed him as aloof compared to more charismatic predecessors.
